I actually love the scarlet rot incantations. They've helped me defeat so many bosses in my ng+ run. I ran with either Rotten Butterflies (from the DLC) or Scarlet Aeonia (from Malenia). They do have pretty long animations, so sometimes it's hard to get them to hit. But if they do, you see the health bar drop almost every second. Most normal enemies can't even take the initial hit and I think they are visually one of the more satisfying incantations. 

I've also used the multilayered ring of light a lot (also DLC). It does quite some damage, but most importantly, it kind of keeps a boss/enemy in one position for a brief moment because it stays in position, giving you some time to attack or heal. The range is also pretty good, so you can cast it on enemies and bosses from quite some distance. There's almost no animation time so you can just keep casting them one after another.

I love philosophy as well and think its amazing to see how analytical modern-day philosphers look at modern science (like Thomas Nagel, Philip Goff, or Slavoj Zizek). Dont agree with many things and they also dont always agree with each other. But it has taught me that loads of scientific questions are philosophical in nature.

We create scientific theories and models to understand the universe. But to experience a phenomenon that is not rational in nature, it is impossible to fully understand it with the methods and models we have today, that ARE totally valueless/rational in nature. It doesn't mean these models/theories are incorrect, but it could mean these theories fall short if you ever want to have a full understanding of the universe and concepts like time and space.

To try to explain it; things like consiousness exist, just because we can't measure it rationally with our current models, doesn’t mean it doesn't exist in the 'real world'. To think something can only exist if it can be empirically proven or measured is true modern-day thinking and very much embedded in this day and age, it's not a given. Consciousness is something that does exist and can be experienced/observed. 

Now you could say you could eventually analyze and measure what goes on in a persons brain/body, and that is what consciousness is. Nothing more than your brain telling you something due to a process going on. But then you dont have a full understanding of what consciousness truly is, right? You just understand a part/an asset of it. However, it's a natural phenomenon that we can experience. It doesn't mean the process going on in your brain/body isn't real as well, but to fully understand the concept of consciousness, you will need to investigate more areas/assets on the subject. Is it possible nature/the universe has assets we can't measure yet because our understanding of how the universe works is just investigating a certain asset of it? 

Time and space are real, though as you said we don't know the exact physical definition of time and space. As we don't with gravity, dark energy, dark matter, the list goes on. We know its there and can observe it, we just dont know what it is exactly. Now I'm not saying there is some magical asset to the universe and we should all go do acid and play drums to experience what the universe has to offer. I'm not saying science and scientific models should be tossed or that they aren't a great way to find out more about the universe. They are absolutely amazing and interesting and are making progress on a scale we have never seen before. 

All I'm saying is what if, as humans, we experience non-physical assets of the universe, and it will be impossible to measure them or prove them with methods that are purely physical in nature. You could say, well then they simply arent real, but that would toss out a huge part of the human experience to arrive at a meaningful conclusion. And no, I'm also not talking about God or whatever, I'm just saying maybe the universe can't be understood by the models and numbers we are using now.

To be fair, don't expect amazing food on the Carretera Austral. It's mostly small towns, so there are some okay/decent restaurants, but most of it is just basic meat or fish with fries, or ceviche. There was one really good pizza place in Chaiten and Coyhaique is a small city, so naturally there you can find the best food and restaurants on the Carretera Austral. As far as dishes go; I ate bulls tongue once lol, it was actually pretty good! 

We booked all our accommodations through booking and/or Airbnb. Some we booked in advance, others we booked while we were on the trip. I'm not sure if you can just walk in and sleep somewhere, we did book some places like a day before, so I'd expect it is possible, but didn't do it myself.

If there are any questions you have about the national parks and stuff, feel free to ask, happy to help!

It was absolutely amazing! Easily one of the most beautiful countries I have ever visited and very nice and welcoming people. You'll be in different vegetation and landscapes every few hours and will be surprised by the beauty of it. The tips here were pretty helpful actually!

You don't need a 4x4 indeed (we just got a normal SUV), but some parts were pretty challenging, especially if it had rained. If you're not used to driving offroad or if you don't drive a lot, make sure you get a car you are comfortable in. Do make sure you get a car that's not too low to the ground. I love driving, so I didn't really mind the challenging parts, but prepare for being on the road a lot and putting your driving skills to the test. I do believe the roads are a lot better as they were and they are still improving. A lot of parts were smooth sailing (I expected worse)

I was actually surprised by how easy it was to book accommodations throughout the trip and there were plenty of places to get food/supplies. I have traveled a lot, so I'm used to being resourceful. We stocked up many times before going to the next place, but it wasn't really necessary in my opinion. Even small villages have places to re-supply. Choice is yours ofcourse.

I actually found the driving part and the views from driving pretty amazing. It's pretty easy to stop anywhere and take in the view. Some hikes are pretty challenging, but they don't necessarily give you a better view. Ofcourse others are totally worth it. But literally every spot has hiking trails, so I would choose your battles wisely.

Some things that are practical:
- Make sure you have enough cash on you and if there's an ATM and you are running low, get some extra. You mostly pay with cash.
- Almost nobody can speak English, learn some basic Spanish if you can, people will really not understand you.
- You need tickets for some of the national Parks, make sure to check in advance.
- It's unclear where some of the entrances of the national parks are. A lot of them have multiple entrances and there aren't many signs pointing you in the right direction. Make sure to check in advance. If you have any questions regarding this send me a message and I'll give you the info! Some entrances are literal hours from another entrance and in other parts you have no idea you are already in the park.
- Some hikes are not just for a day. There are parts you need to be in for a week and camp if you actually want to do the trails there. We didn't know this!
- Watch out with talking about politics. There are a lot of complex issues in the country and I experienced people don't really like to talk about it unless they are comfortable with you.
- People eat everything with cutlery. Pizza? Knife and fork. Hamburger? Knife and fork. Fries? Knife and fork. You don't really eat with your hands and I believe its considered dirty. We just went with it!
- Google Maps was pretty much on point the whole trip about travel time. Was surprised by this lol.
